During a cricket match a batter hits shots A and B, shown on the diagram below. Both shots
achieve the same maximum height above the ground but shot B travels twice as far horizontally.

Which quantity below is DIFFERENT for shots A and B? Circle your response.

Time of Flight
Initial Velocity
Final Vertical Speed

Briefly explain why your chosen quantity is correct and why the others are not.
text: During a cricket match a batter hits shots A and B, shown on the diagram below. Both shots achieve the same maximum height above the ground but shot B travels twice as far horizontally. Which quantity below is DIFFERENT for shots A and B? Circle your response. Time of Flight Initial Velocity Final Vertical Speed Briefly explain why your chosen quantity is correct and why the others are not.
answerHtml:
Which quantity below is DIFFERENT for shots A and B? Circle your response.
Briefly explain why your chosen quantity is correct and why the others are not.

Description

Since the max heights are equal, the time of flight of
A and B are equal (t A=t B).

Since the vertical velocities of A and B are equal, the
time of flight of A and B are equal (t A=t B).

As the horizontal range is doubled, the horizontal
velocity of shot B must be double the horizontal
velocity of shot A (since the time is same).

ux ,B=2 ux , A

Hence, since the horizontal component of initial
velocity of B is double A and the vertical components
are the same, the initial velocity will be different.

Artificial Gravity in Space

There have been various attempts over the years to design spacecraft that mimic the Earth’s
gravity for astronauts. All such designs are aimed at providing artificial gravity that astronauts can
experience while in space. The benefit of producing artificial gravity is to reduce some of the
negative effects of long periods of weightlessness, such as the weakening of bones and muscles
responsible for movement.

On earth we rely on the force due to gravity to pull us down while the ground supplies an upwards
reaction force. One way to imitate gravity in space is to use the centripetal force provided by a
rotating space station. If an astronaut is rotated within a space station, then “up” is towards the
centre of rotation and “down” is into the floor. The only force exerted on the astronaut is the floor
pushing “up”. This force is the centripetal force acting on the astronaut as they rotate. The artificial
gravity experienced is the centripetal acceleration.

For a set rotation rate, the artificial gravity increases with greater distance from the axis of rotation.
Therefore, small-diameter structures would need to rotate at high rates to provide an artificial
gravity of “1g” (where “1g” is the acceleration due to gravity experienced on the surface of the
Earth). To simulate artificial gravity of “1g” at a rotation rate of 1 rpm, a very large structure would
be needed. From a human perspective, rotation rates greater than 5 rpm tend to cause imbalance
in the sensitive organs in our ears.

Figure 1 – NASA’s concept spacecraft, the Nautilus X (source: Wikipedia)

One such system is that of a rotating torus in NASA’s advanced spacecraft the Nautilus-X. Shown
in Figure 1, one segment is a 12.2 m diameter torus (donut shape) that can rotate at 10 rpm,
allowing astronauts to experience artificial gravity of about “1g” while in space.

Figure 2 below shows an astronaut rotating with a spacecraft. It can be shown that the amount of
artificial gravity ga experienced by the astronaut rotating in a spacecraft is given by ga=4 π

two habitats (a habitat being a place where astronauts can live) tethered to one end of the main
spacecraft structure and the engines at the other end of the structure. The entire structure is then
rotated about its centre of mass. Figure 3 shows a schematic for the Mars Transfer Vehicle (MTV),
having two habitats positioned 112 m apart, spinning at 4 rpm.

Figure 3 – schematic of the MTV

In both systems (Figure 1 and Figure 3) the rotating person is projected towards the outside of
either the habitat or torus ring and the spacecraft provides a reaction force, thus simulating gravity.

Millikan’s Oil Drop Experiment

In 1909 Robert Millikan and Harvey Fletcher performed an experiment to measure the elementary
electric charge on an electron. As shown in Figure 4 below, the experiment involved observing very
small electrically charged oil droplets move between two parallel metal plates. These two metal
plates formed a capacitor with an electric field between them.

Figure 4 – schematic for Millikan’s experiment

When oil is sprayed into the chamber a fine mist of very small, charged oil droplets is created
within. Due to the very small size of the oil droplets, they gradually fall under their own weight,
some entering the space between the two parallel plates.

With the voltage supply turned on, an electric field is created between the parallel plates separated
by distance d. When this happens the oil droplets rise at a constant velocity vup. At this velocity the
electric force (F E) upwards is balanced by the downward forces of the weight of the oil droplet (W )
and the drag force (Ddown) on the droplet moving through the air.

To calculate the weight of each droplet, Millikan then turned off the voltage supply and watched the
oil droplet fall, at a constant velocity vdown. At this speed the downward weight force (W ) of the
droplet is balanced by the upward drag force (Dup) on the droplet as it moves down through the air.

The forces acting on the oil droplets, when the voltage is on and off, are shown in Figure 5 below.

Figure 5 – forces acting on an oil droplet

From the measurements of vup and vdown, and from knowing that drag forces increase with velocity,
Millikan could calculate the total charge on many oil droplets. Millikan assumed (correctly) that
each oil droplet contained a charge equal to an integer multiple of the elementary charge on an
electron. Millikan assumed that the smallest charge difference observed was the elementary
charge and any larger charge difference were integer multiples of this elementary charge.

To determine a value for the elementary charge on an electron, some Physics students set up a
similar apparatus where the distance between the parallel plates d =16.0 mm. The students then
applied a high voltage supply V , injected some charged oil droplets, measured the upwards
velocity vup, switched off the voltage and measured the downwards velocity vdown.

The results of their experiment are recorded below in Table 1.

Table 1 – Results for Students’ Oil Drop Experiment
